text: All right. Good evening. I'm calling to order the Performance Monitoring Committee meeting for Tuesday, June 2nd, 2026. I am joined by Ms. April Chandler of Algonquin and Ms. Lauren Shurnoff of Leesburg. Tonight, we're going to be reviewing a couple of information items here on the stakeholder survey results and the data dashboard discussion. We have no public comment, I see. So we're going to move on to 3.0, the meeting

minutes. Do I have a motion to approve the meeting minutes from our last meeting for May 5th, 2026? So moved. Second. Second. Thank you. It was moved by Ms. Shurnoff and seconded by Ms. Chandler, and those meeting minutes are approved. All in favor say aye. Aye. Aye. Great, and the meeting minutes have been approved. We'll move on to 4.0, our information items.

The Department of Academics is presenting on the annual stakeholder survey results, and I will turn the floor over to you guys. Thank you, Ms. Cardy. Thank you for having me here this evening to talk about the annual survey. I'm going to walk through some of the results today. So if we could move to the next slide. So just a quick overview. Survey window is open from February 19th to March 17th. We deploy the survey a couple different

ways. For families, we send an email out to the first two contacts in ParentVUE for every school in which they have a child enrolled. For school-based staff, we send them an email as well. Students actually log in through a public URL by entering their student ID, and that methodology allows for single taking of the survey only. Things we want to talk about with that is that we send out reminders

throughout the survey period, so that should only go to non-participants. We also sit and provide technical assistance. We receive many emails about not finding links, things like that. So we support participants that way. We do translate our family and student surveys into our top five languages, being Arabic, Farsi, Spanish, Vietnamese, and Urdu. And then for some schools, we do have some paper surveys upon request. We'll send them the template, and then we'll manually enter those data as

well. Before we actually get into it, I do want to talk a little bit about how reporting is rolled out as well. So this is kind of the bookends of it. So we do reporting internally where we create a Qlik app for division-level staff, and from there, we create separate Qlik apps for principals to be able to review their own data. We give them some time to review and process their data, and then we open it up to all staff. And then the next phase after that is we put out our public PDFs on our research website so people can see all the results

by each school. So if we can move on to the next slide. So what we're looking at here is going to be the participation. Couple of things that are noteworthy here is that the high school students, they take the Virginia Department of Education School Climate Survey. It's high schoolers this year, middle schoolers next year. And whichever group does not take that survey, they take our survey. So we'll go back and forth, and that'll come up again in a little bit. In terms of participation, I would say this is probably the best

participation by students that I've seen since I've been here in four years. School-based staff is pretty strong as well. Families, we've seen some waning participation from families on our surveys as well. That said, it's a little bit of a balance because we don't want to dismiss the opinions of those who did take the survey, but at the same time, think about how widespread those perceptions are. So if we could move to the next slide.

So the way we're going to go through this part of it is we're going to go through strengths and opportunities for improvement. And strengths are going to be defined by the top five highest percentage of combined 'agreement' and 'strongly agree' responses. When we look at the calculations, we do not exclude the 'don't know' from the calculations. We include them in that because when we look at agreement, these are the people who are actively saying these things are happening, and that's what we want to focus on for this.

On this slide, we have that for this year, and then we also have the three-year trend as well. So you can see that these are pretty consistent across the three years as well. And really the emphasis, the theme from these items is going to be on safety and respect. So if we go to the next slide. So conversely, this is the highest percentage of 'strongly disagree' and 'disagree.' And we do that for one reason, is that

we want to make sure that the 'don't know' doesn't dilute anything. As well as these are the people who are actively saying these things are not happening. So similar to last slide, the three-year trend is shown. And really what we're seeing here as far as the focus of these items is going to be on feedback, whether it be the school on student work, academic risks, and consistency. Go to the next slide. Very similar concept with the top five items.

Really, we're looking at the primary theme here being staff supporting each other as well as supporting students. So we have a high level of agreement around those two concepts. And on the next slide, we're looking to deal with the disagreement pieces. It has to do with planning time, time to plan and collaborate, as well as discipline, specifically consistent enforcement and student awareness of consequences, and that's going to come back in just a few moments.

It is important to note that there's been steady improvement on each of these areas over the last three years. So you can see that we want the disagreement to decrease, and we're seeing that happen across these items.So looking at the middle school students survey, as a reminder, they take the survey every other year. That's why they only have two years on here. We're looking at the theme of basically positive relationships with teachers and peers.

One thing to point out is the different student's perspective between middle school students and staff about students knowing their consequences for their actions. If you look back on the teacher one, on the previous one, the staff one, that was one of the highest levels of disagreement. Here it's one of the highest levels of agreement. So we're seeing some disconnect between those two concepts. If we move on to the next slide. That said, we also see some consistency with that

consistent enforcement of discipline between staff members and middle schoolers. So the other thing that's important to point out is the improvement that we see in students treating each other with respect, regardless of race or other differences, as well as school cleanliness. Looking at the next slide, for elementary students, really the big strengths are going to be around peer and student relationships, so relationships with each other.

You'll see those ones up there that do not have another one with them. There's ones on the middle school. Those are new items that we added this year. That's going to be part of the belonging scale, which I'll talk about in just a moment or two. But we can see very high percentages on those. And then on the next slide, what we're going to see here is that similar to all the others, the staff, as well as the middle school students, that consistency and discipline has that high level of disagreement that we're looking at across those three populations as well.

So that's sort of the general through line across school-based staff, middle school students, and elementary school students. So if we move on to the next slide, and this is the introduction of our belonging scale. What we did is we created 16 items based on information that's in the literature, as well combined with some of the sample survey items in the book, "Belonging and a Culture of Dignity."

And so we combine those. When we're looking to develop a scale, we're going to create more items than we think we need, and then we'll do some analysis over the summer to see if that needs to be pared down at all to see if there's some overlap. Really the themes of the items in the belonging scale are going to be about relationships with teachers, relationship with peers, and access and participation in different activities as well. Next up is going to be our net promoter score.

So when we're looking at the net promoter, we're thinking about an individual's connection to a concept. It can also be used as a proxy for trust and/or employee engagement. So in this case, what we're looking at here is that each of these is... I'm sorry, the family one is down a little bit from last year, but it still falls into the good category. And then the division level net promoter score from staff members is up from 30 last year, so it's up two points. We're seeing some progress there.

And then on the last slide is going to be the school level net promoter score. This is the first year we asked the students the net promoter score question. We know middle schoolers all love school, so there should be no surprises here. That said, the families and staff ones are down just a point from last year, but in this case, they would fall into the great category. So we're still seeing some very positive movement there. So with that said, I know I just walked through survey

results very quickly. There's a lot of items, and that's why I focused on the strengths and opportunities and for improvement concept. But with that, I will open it up to any questions. Thank you so much. You want to start? Okay. Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you so much for the presentation. I'm curious, I believe this is something that's been happening within the division for quite some time.

Do we ever take a look at what the trends indicate beyond three years? If you were to reflect on what the perceptions were 10 or 15 years ago, would we have access to data that could give us that information? So that's a great question, and one of the things to consider to that is how long have we been administering the survey in this form? Which has been for a number of years, but usually we've got up to I think four years in our survey platform right now, which

is where we pull the data. We could probably look back a few years beyond that, but the survey has changed a bit when I got here four years ago. And so what we'd need is we would need, what are the constant questions that we've seen across those, and we could certainly take a look into doing that. I wouldn't say we'd be able to go much beyond five years, though. And I would add to it that the sense of belonging and the equity work really took hold maybe six or seven years ago.

So 10 or 15 years ago, we weren't necessarily collecting belonging data, and we weren't as deep conceptual until the equity work. So some of the questions and concepts are relatively new in the last six or seven years. Okay, thank you. Thank you. Go ahead. Go for it. Thank you, Madam Chair, and thank you guys for the presentation. I think middle schoolers are hilarious.

Especially right now with my two going out the door every morning like, "Ugh, no more." So I just thought that gave me a chuckle because middle school, it's just a tough time in a kid's life. I want to thank Dr. Ellis for getting back to me earlier in the week because really, to me, this overarching data tells us some things. We're doing a generally pretty good job, and I really appreciate the consistency that we're seeing across.

It is a lot concerning to me that less than 10% of our families are responding. I don't know what that means, if maybe-One could wonder if they're happy, and so they don't feel like they need to fill that out, or they just have survey fatigue, so maybe we should give them a survey to find out. No, I'm just kidding. But we have been giving a lot of surveys recently, so I found that interesting. But I actually find the school-based data to be really fascinating, especially to hear from our students.

And, I think the schools have gotten really strategic in making sure that they take the survey during advisory or at a certain point of the day to ensure that kids are having a chance to respond so that we really can see that. And I had asked earlier in the week where the data lives for the individual schools, and so if you all could just share that for the public, I think that that is an important point of reference. Thank you for that. And to that point, so the individual unit of analysis

for the survey is the school. So it's all about the school that they're in. So the school-level data is going to be what's key in this. Right now, we have the survey data in Qlik apps inside of our own business intelligence software for principals to review, and that will be available for staff. For the public-facing view of it, what we will do is probably by the end of the month, we will generate a PDF for each survey, for each population, for each school, that will be posted on

the research website that's available for the public to see. We'll also try to put out some information about an overall survey summary. But ultimately, we have the school data living on the research website, for people to be able to go there and look at the data for their own school. I appreciate that. And I believe last year's is still up because I was digging around. Oh, you pulled it up. Awesome. Yep. So I did pull it up. So if you go to the research webpage on

the LCPS site and click on Surveys. And then you'll get our beautiful division-wide survey calendar that Dr. Blake-Locke maintains. And then if you scroll down to the bottom, you'll see the '24-'25 school climate survey reports. There's a folder. I'm assuming you'll use the same format. There's a folder for each school, and then inside each folder, you'll see a summary document of each survey.

That is helpful. And I'm very curious about getting to the micro level of all of that, much like I've spoken in the past about achievement data. It's great that overall LCPS is thriving, but there are things that get disguised in that overall overarching data. And so I guess my question is twofold. It's sort of, so what and now what? So what does it tell us and then what does that spur us to do? So if someone could speak a little bit to the process that goes on behind the

scenes, maybe at looking at that individual school climate data. Is there a pattern of looking back across years and seeing if trends change? Leadership does change in our schools, curriculums change, different initiatives come in. I would be interested to know what the county does with that data on a more micro level to address potential supports. So I'll take the first run at this and then pass it on.

So basically what will happen is that the way that principals and school staff are able to look at the data is that they are able to compare how they did this year to the year previous and what that change looks like, as well as how they compare to all the other schools at their school level. So they can see that context of where they fit into the whole and how they've changed over time. This year, we actually put out some PDFs to them for them to be able to stand in front of their staff to present, that actually had three years of data because

people kept on asking me to download data from the Qlik app. So we just created reports for them. So schools will actually use that to inform their school improvement plans. They will look at the areas where they need to grow and their strengths, and they will actually use that to inform their school improvement plans over the course of the next year. I'm going to pass it to some of my colleagues at the table to speak a little bit further about ways they could also be used. Thanks, Dr. Blake-Locke. So in addition to everything that he just said, I'll just add that the

Department of School Leadership, specifically the level directors and the executive principals, use that data in conversations with the principals as they coach and evaluate the principals. While it's not specifically used in the evaluation process in terms of using the survey to set goals for the principal, we don't recommend principals do that. It's a really important part of the conversation. And to your point, as

leadership changes in a school, it's really helpful for a new principal to have all of this information in front of them when they start in a new building, set their own goals for how they're going to work with their students, their families, and their staff. So that's another key way. So I would say school improvement process and then in coaching conversations with the principals. I appreciate that. And I think as we wrap up the year,

looking at some of that transition data, looking at whether people are staying or going, and whether or not that has to do with climate, and then thinking about achievement. I think you could put a lot of layers here, especially for, really, we are saying belonging matters here in Loudoun County Public Schools, and that that's what kids need in order to learn. And is our data telling us that? Is that something that we're seeing? And I think we've talked about it before in PMC prior to it changing over. But are the schools that have

high achievement, do they also have a high sense of belonging? Are there schools that have a high sense of belonging and low achievement? And how are we connecting all these dots? So I'd be curious. And I just had one other food for thought. It's curious to me that families and students seem to be in the disagree and the strongly disagree, that they're talking a lot about feedback loops. And so to me, I wasReflecting on this and wondering also, it made me think about the

walkthrough data we did for the instructional framework and how the weakness we saw there or an area for growth is goal setting. And I was thinking about how those two things could really strengthen one another. So if we can get really good at students knowing what they need to learn, how to set a goal, how to then reach their goal in that feedback loop, and then communicating that out back to the students and also to the families, I think that could be a two for one, and that's just my food for thought for the day.

Definitely. Can I add one tiny tidbit to your- Sure. ... food for thought? So I also think I'm connecting it to just things I've been thinking about in multiple conversations I've had over the past several weeks, is how do we close that feedback loop? Because we get that feedback a lot that we don't seek input, or staff don't feel their voices are heard, or et cetera. On the flip side, I think people in our office

think they are constantly asking for feedback and input. We have tons of examples of that. But how do we close the loop to let people know how we used their feedback, right? Just because we have gathered feedback doesn't mean you're going to see it in your own words in the final product. But it's important information to have, and your ideas have been incorporated, but I don't know that that final closing of the loop always happens.

Yeah. It's definitely food for thought. Yeah. And just being on this committee, and we get a lot of data every time we're together, but it's like some of these things are now starting to connect for me at a higher level of like, "Ooh, that's a trend." And yeah, we are seeing that outside of school too. That's how families also feel. So those could be some common threads, I think, as a school board, that we could take and say, "This really needs support." And whether that's directing the superintendent operationally or that's something that we can do with finances

or initiatives, I think that that's something that's worth exploring in terms of how we can leverage this kind of data. So that's it. Thanks. Anything else you want to add, too? Sure. So just in reflecting on the participation rate for families, has there been any discussion about what we could do to try to overcome this participation rate, or what opportunities we have for engaging in a different way to collect more information?

So one thing I failed to mention during my presentation was that there is a very comprehensive communications campaign that we put out. We put out newsletters, we create principal toolkits, we put out social media posts. We do a lot to broadcast it out there. I do think to some extent, getting better at closing the loop, like we were just talking about, would help it so people can understand the impact of their feedback. And Dr. Tyler and I were recently having some discussions about sort of an innovative

way to do that. Don't want to reveal that in this conversation here, so be on the edge of your seat. But it's the one thing we haven't tried yet that may be available to us, just because to your point, I would say just based on work I've done previously, in a large district like this, 10% is probably the minimum you want to see given that 122,000, that's 12,000 responses. And we've been above that before my time here.

But really trying to see what we can do to try to get people more engaged. And it's more than just regurgitating back what we've heard, but also being able to deliver to them this is the change that occurred based on that feedback as well, this was the impact of your feedback. So it is something we are working on. Those in the research office know that as soon as that survey goes out, I'm checking participation rate five times a day. We do put out what's known as participation reports to the level directors and

executive principals so that they can see participation level by school. So if there's a place that they want to try to push or try to support, that's data that's available for them as well, and that's a dynamic report that they get real time every time they click it. And I do think that helped the staff and student participation rate this year. The challenge is reaching families, and it comes out in newsletters and all the ways that we communicate with families.

The one thing I'll add to that, too, is that that's going to be two contacts at least per student. So maybe one parent takes it, but not the other. So there is a little bit of wiggle room in there. Is it the 7% being truly 7% of our total population, or if it's going to be a little higher than that because only one contact took it and not the other.

Thank you, guys, for this. This is really interesting information, as always. And I guess one of my questions is just to make sure I understand. So this is all sense of belonging questions. Do we have all-- No? So slide 12 is the sense of belonging- Got it ... specific question. Okay. The rest of it is going to be questions from across all the domains in the survey. It's just going to be the highest five agreement and the highest five disagreement, just for sake of brevity in this presentation.

Okay. Could we get a list of all of the questions and all-- You said you guys are going to post it. Do you post all the questions and all the results in that? Okay. Yes, we will post all of that. The last one. Okay. Yeah, that'll be really helpful. I think also on the website where you guys post the results, I think it'd be really great for you to post some of the bullets that were outcomes from last year's underneath there. So you can say, "Well, this is the survey that was taken, and based on these results, these are the however many action things that we took from it, and

this is how we've implemented it." That way, it's where the results are and people can say, "Oh, this is what they did with that information." That might be a good place to put that. And probably others, too, but I think that might be a good start. I guess one of my questions I have-- I have a bunch of questions about this, and I always find surveying questions and just the survey process is interesting, too. And I'm wondering ifIf we're surveying

the right questions that people are wanting to provide feedback for. There's any number of a thousand reasons why the families didn't res-- there's a low response rate for the families, and it could be that there are other questions that they would be more engaged in answering that aren't on here. So, and I'm not sure I know exactly what they are, but that may be something to think about too, is instead of just asking the same questions year to year, which is also helpful to be able to get trends on these things that we're doing well,

I would wonder if now we need to move maybe to some other questions just to stir the pot a little bit as far as the data that we're gathering. And as far as the opportunities go, obviously really interesting as well, and obviously they're mostly moving in the right direction. I'd be really curious about that middle too, and the middle six or so that are in there. You said there are 16 questions? Oh, no. There's 16 questions for the belonging scale alone. Oh, okay. Alone. Okay.

There's probably roughly 30 to 35 questions- In the survey? -per for each of the surveys, yes. Well, bless you guys. No wonder. And- Yeah, that's a lot ... that is something to consider for the participation rate, is that they are long, and seeing if there's anything we can do to pare- Yeah ... them back a little bit, because they are fairly long surveys. Yeah. And they've just got the calendar survey, and they've gotten-- What else have they gotten in this last month or so? They've gotten a few CIP surveys. There's been many surveys throughout the year, and we're trying to pace the calendar for every year.

So we're starting to actually set the calendar for next year right now, so that we can try to create these windows and create some blackout periods around them, so that we're not getting survey after survey. Yeah. 30 questions is a lot. Yeah, it's just interesting. It's hard to crack the nut on survey data and getting people to respond and whatnot. So, but I think it's really good. I would love for us to be able to take a look at this and then again, cross-reference this

against some things, but I'm not sure exactly what to cross-reference it against, which might be a conversation for later in this meeting. But it's definitely good information to have. And then, the net promoter scores, I always find them fascinating and interesting, and just, I'm not sure how much I put a lot of weight in them anymore. But you said that the-- And then again, not having any historical information on here, you said they both went,

the family numbers went down one or up one? Just down a point or two. Okay. For context, the first year that we presented the net promoter score, the school staff one was negative six, negative eight, somewhere in that way. So we've seen a fair amount of growth- That's good ... at least at the division level for the net promoter scores. Yeah. It's just a matter of what does that trend look like over time, and making sure that stays upright. So- Yeah ... maybe next year, middle schoolers will give us something above zero.

Well, yeah. So when we're looking at this and then out years, seeing that kind of growth would be really great to know, because in and of itself, a 47 or a 37 or a negative six, which just makes me laugh at middle schoolers. It's fine, but it's really the context that that sits in and what the historical trends have been that's the real key here. So, and then I'm just going to go back because I looked at this a while ago, but the

school-based staff responses, it's at 42%. That's pretty high. Yeah. And so that tells me a couple things too. Number one, they clearly want to provide feedback, and if they're willing to answer that many questions in a survey, then that's telling too, right? That you've got a huge number of people that want to provide feedback. And so you can slice that a whole bunch of different ways. But it's interesting, and it makes me wonder, are there other questions that we

need to ask them to further flesh out some of the findings, especially with the issues that they're having right now. I know they mention in here, staff prep time was the- Yeah. Not new, and that's fine. And it's obviously getting better because it went from- Yeah ... 66 two years ago, down to 58, which is a good trend, but that's still by and far their

biggest issue. And so then the question becomes, what are we doing right now to help with that? And there are probably initiatives in place for that, but I think with measuring those kind of things and what we're doing action-wise versus how are we continuing to trend and what's going to really move that needle for our school-based staff is really important. So that's all I have on this one. The one data point that we haven't really done a lot with

in this particular report, because it is a fairly cumbersome task to analyze it, is the feedback from the open-ended responses. So we will actually be working on that over the course of the summer. Try to do something a little different with it for this meeting, but I was not able to get it to a position where it was presentation ready. But we will have some folks working on and analyzing and doing thematic analysis, so we get a good understanding and are able to extract and use those data as well. And that might be something similar to the strategic plan

survey, where we break it out from the net promoter score categories, so we get those three different distinct categories, so one is not washing out the perceptions of the other. Yeah. One of my employee engagement survey tools that we use for clients does that, and it's really great to see your unhappy employee or most disengaged employees and what they have to say versus the most engaged and what they have to say. And then the middle is always really fascinating, too. So that may be a really interesting thing to look at as well.

Yeah, I was going to ask you earlier about open-ended, but I forgot about that. So thanks for letting me know that that's on the table as well. What was the biggest aha, and then the one thing that's the most concerning that you've seen out of the results so far? From these particular results, I really can't speak to one way or the other, just coming at it from a pure analytical perspective. The couple of things that really do pop out at me is when we

go back to that feedback on work, timely and helpful, thinking about the implications for how it relates to policy 5030, which I spent a lot of time working with, is one of the things that jumped off the page for me. Looking at some of the pieces around discipline that have been somewhat consistent over the years, as well as that disconnect between how staff feel about discipline and awareness of school rules and those sorts of things, and then how families and students feel

about it, and that disconnect is going to be a connection there. So those are the ones, I said I didn't have any, but those are the ones that are really- Data people always have something. There's always something ... jump off the page at me. Yeah. As well as digging in a little bit more on what net promoter score looks like at the school level. It's something we've not done a ton with, but are looking to advance that. We did something with it for the first time, I think, last year, because to

Ms. Chernov's point, the disaggregation is really where the meat of the data lie, and looking at what that range is from who might be a negative 30 and who might be a positive 80 across the school, from both across the continuum for both families and staff members. It's not analysis we've done yet, but it's interesting things that we've seen in it and what we've done in the past. Do we have any demographic data for these survey results, too? Do we collect that at the beginning so that we know anything about the

students or the people that are responding? It depends. So we have demographics data for the students. For families, it is self-report, and there's a prefer not to answer option with it as well. So we get a rough idea of at least how many of a particular group have taken it, but we don't get a true proportion because of that prefer not to answer piece. For staff members, we ask, I think we ask length of service is going to be it, and whether or not they're instructional staff, because that drives some of the skip logic inside of the survey.

That'll be really fascinating because what we see in industry is early career, pretty engaged, then a big drop off of the five to 10 year, and then a re-engagement from 11 to 15 years, and then a plateauing beyond that. So it'll be really fascinating to see how that trends to what we get here. So engagement work I've done in my previous life as a consultant, very similar- Yeah ... as far as first-year teachers that are out to change the world are engaged up

until five years, and then other life events start happening and engagement drips off, and then maybe there's more less responsibilities, and it starts picking up there around 15, 20 years- Yeah ... in that period as well. So very similar trend we're seeing. Yeah. It'll be very interesting to see that. Thank you guys so much for this. Anything else on this one? Mm-mm. All right. Let's move along to the next.

Yeah, somewhere in here. Yep. So we're at 4.02. So this is data dashboard discussion. All right. So I will kick us off and then turn it over to Mr. Smith and Dr. Blake-Lach to talk through some of the details. So this really is meant to just be a quick follow-up to our conversation at our last meeting, and we wanted to talk a little bit about the

dashboard categories that staff is now thinking of based on your feedback and discussion. And we have some updates in terms of our plans for this summer, what we will be working on with the phase one data elements, and then Mr. Smith has an update for you on our data modernization project. So just as a reminder, this is what we started with last time we talked. We had six categories and multiple data elements inside each

category. We talked about splitting them up, collapsing them, having three, having 12. This is sort of where we've landed based on all of that conversation, which was really helpful for us to think about. So we're thinking high level students, staff, family and community, and operations and finance. Within students, we think it's really important to separate

achievement, engagement and belonging, and enrollment data. There are enough discrete pieces of data in each of these buckets that we would have a category for each, but we also want to avoid having the user have to click, click, click through many layers. So starting with those four buckets of students, staff, family and community, and operations and finance. So what we would do is ultimately take
